newsitem.title: USA: USDA unlikely to revive EEP anytime soon - official.
newsitem.headline: USDA unlikely to revive EEP anytime soon - official.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Department is unlikely to revive the Export Enhancement Program anytime soon despite a recent subsidized wheat sale by the European Union, a USDA official said.

"It's unlikely that our policy is going to change unless the EU demonstrates that they are entertaining a more aggressive export program for this year," said the official, who asked not to be identified.
USDA shelved the EEP more than a year ago, around the same time the European Union put its subsidy program on hold. High prices and low stocks were also factors.
Last week, EU subsidized a wheat sale to African, Caribbean and Pacific countries (ACP) raising questions whether USDA might dust off the EEP.
"Obviously we took note of what the EU did, but it's not anything of significance," the USDA official said, noting that sales to those countries had been subsidized all along.

"Right now, it's just kind of a watch and see situation for us," the USDA official said. "We're going to look and monitor what the EU is doing and they know that we are prepared if necessary to respond if they were to engage in a progressively aggressive export campaign."
The USDA official noted that prices for wheat were still strong around the world and that until more of the harvest took place competition would be low.
EU is facing similiar financial constraints to using export subsidies as USDA, whose FY97 budget for EEP was shaved to $100 million under the 1996 Farm Bill, the official added.
The USDA official also pointed out that U.S. exports were running ahead of last year without subsidies and that that sales pace was expected to continue.

Agriculture industry sources said they were skeptical the U.S. would re-institute EEP this marketing year due to tight supplies, the poor crop, food price inflation concerns and limited funding for the subsidy program.
"It would be pretty hard to use government money to discount feedgrains when you've got cattle people complaining," said one.
USDA recently sold grain to raise money to aid livestock producers hardhit by drought and high cattle feed prices.

Another industry source said while it was widely believed that the EU would use subsidies at some point this marketing year given their decent crop, the ACP sale showed the EU was not being "terribly aggressive" at the moment since these were preferred countries with historical ties. -- Leila Corcoran, Washington Commodities, 202-898-8394
